transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2028-06-17 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (SentinelCore CTO), Priya Nair (Lead ML Eng), Daniel Kim (Infra), Aisha Rahman (Product)

Summary (auto): weekly perf checkpoint focused on head-to-head metrics vs incumbent; discuss tuning and next steps.

[00:00] Jordan Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, quick roll call — Jordan here, Maya on the line, uh thanks for taking time.
[00:10] Liam O'Connor: Yep, Liam here. Priya, Daniel — we're good.
[00:15] Maya Chen: Great. I'll start with the numbers we ran overnight, and then we'll dig into the config tweaks.
[02:15] Maya Chen: So high level — under the test harness (the sentinel benchmark suite you shared) our p50 for short chat prompts is ~78ms versus the incumbent's 120ms, p95 is ~240ms vs 380ms. p99 is still a bit high at ~520ms vs incumbent 490ms, so tail's where we need to zero in. There was some variance during synthetic bursts.
[05:10] Priya Nair: Wait — p99 520? that's surprising, we were expecting more consistent tails. Can you remind us of the setup? batch sizes, KV cache warm, quantization profile?
[05:40] Maya Chen: Yeah, setup: model is open-llama-v2-13b-equivalent, quantized to int8-ops (we used Redwood Optimize's suggested profile Q8-fast). Batching policy was dynamic batching with 32ms window, KV-cache warm for 95% of requests. The burst scenario we ran was a 60s ramp to 800 rps which pushed batching behaviour and the kernel selector sometimes to the fp16 fallback path.
[09:00] Daniel Kim: On our side, the incumbent is using smaller batches but more reserved capacity so their tail is flatter. Curious if we can match that with dedicated slots.
[09:30] Jordan Patel: Right — that's why we're going to propose a dedicated 2x-GPU slot to reduce kernel switching. It makes scheduling more predictable and reduces context switching overhead. But of course tradeoff is cost.
[11:05] Liam O'Connor: Cost is important. Our baseline unit-cost to host is 0.013 token-unit from incumbent, what does Redwood look like at similar throughput?
[11:25] Jordan Patel: I'll share a cost model in the follow-up CSV but at the throughput we saw with caching and batching optimizations, unit cost is about 8-12% lower. If you take dedicated reserved slots there is an up-front commit but per-token goes down further.
[13:20] Priya Nair: Hmm ok, can you clarify the fallback behavior? If the dedicated pool fills, will requests go to hosted variants and does that preserve data isolation?
[13:40] Maya Chen: Yes — routing policy can be set to degrade to a private hosted variant with enforced data-at-rest encryption, but for strict isolation you'd pin to Dedicated only. We also support automated fallback with redaction — but audit logs will show the fallback events.
[18:05] Priya Nair: On security: SOC 2 and KMS integration — do you surface which KMS was used for key operations in audit logs? We need proof for our compliance team.
[18:35] Jordan Patel: We do. The private deployment includes audit records for KMS operations, key IDs, and per-request metadata. We'll attach the security pack.
[22:40] Maya Chen: Back to the bench: we dug into kernel selection logs and saw a couple of paths where attention kernels were reverted to a generic slower kernel under certain sequence-length spikes. We think a small change to max-seq cutoff and a slightly larger batching window prevented the fallback in our next run.
[25:00] Daniel Kim: Can you quantify impact of that tweak?
[25:10] Maya Chen: Sure — after increasing the batching window from 32ms to 45ms and adjusting max sequence branch to 512 vs a previous 384, p95 dropped from 240ms to ~198ms, p99 improved to ~420ms on the controlled 800rps burst test. Throughput steady-state improved ~12%.
[30:12] Liam O'Connor: That sounds promising, but for production we'd want to test with our mixed-length traffic profile. We'll run the 72-hour mixed workload next sprint.
[30:40] Maya Chen: Perfect — also note we saw token-emit jitter for long-form completions when quantization profile set to Q8-fast; switching to the Q8-stable profile smoothed throughput but raised p50 by about 6ms. Tradeoff again.
[33:50] Priya Nair: So tradeoffs: Q8-fast better p50/p95 but more jitter on long sequences; Q8-stable smoother but slightly higher median. For our use case (low-latency chat + some long summaries) maybe a hybrid routing: route long seq requests to a stable profile node. Can Redwood route by sequence length?
[34:20] Maya Chen: Yes, routing by request attributes is supported — you can tag routes (long-form vs short-chat) and assign model/quant profiles per route.
[36:55] Daniel Kim: Any gotchas with KV cache across fallbacks? We rely heavily on prefix caching for short chats. If a request is rerouted mid-conversation, do we lose the cache or is it duplicated?
[37:20] Maya Chen: Good question. The KV cache is local to the instance. If fallback occurs to a different model variant the cache won't be reused automatically. We have an optional shared prefix cache that can be enabled on Dedicated which mitigates this, but it adds memory and cost.
[40:05] Aisha Rahman: Are there observability hooks we can push into our SRE stack? We want per-route traces and token-level cost breakdowns.
[40:20] Jordan Patel: Redwood Console exports per-route traces, token-level cost, and you can stream traces to your datadog or prometheus endpoint. We'll include example dashboards in the follow-up.
[42:10] Priya Nair: Ok for actionability: we'll run the 72-hour mixed-length workload with both Q8-fast and Q8-stable, and with/without shared prefix cache. We'll also try a dedicated 2x slot for a 4-hour window to see tail behavior.
[46:05] Jordan Patel: Great. Recap — Jordan to send annotated CSV and pricing, Maya to schedule kernel deep-dive, Priya to share target SLA and initiate the 72-hour test. Any final questions?
[46:25] Liam O'Connor: None here, thanks.
[46:35] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in the thread.
[46:45] Meeting end.
